text: 2.1 The chessboard is composed of an 8 x 8 grid of 64 equal squares alternately light (the ‘white’ squares) and dark (the ‘black’ squares). The chessboard is placed between the players in such a way that the near corner square to the right of the player is white.

This exchange of a pawn for another piece is called promotion, and the effect of the new piece is immediate.

Before looking at some of the more common openings played today it is important to consider what you are trying to achieve in the opening of a chess game.
In some cases, one player will sacrifice a pawn, or in some cases even more, to accomplish the goals listed below. Such an opening is called a gambit.

Development You should attempt to move your pieces away from their starting positions to squares in which they can participate more fully in the game. Obviously a Knight at c3 is more effective both defensively and aggressively than a knight on b1. Avoid moving pieces more than once in the opening as this allows your opponent time to develop another piece while you are wasting time. Also avoid moving your queen in the opening, it can too easily be chased around the board by other pieces which aids your opponent's development while wasting moves for you.

Control the Centre The squares in the centre of the board are critical for two reasons. The first is that pieces in the centre are able to move to more squares than pieces on the edges. (Note a knight on a3 can move to only 4 squares, whereas a knight on c3 can move to 8.) Secondly, if you control the centre it is easier to move pieces from Kingside to Queenside quickly.

One of the great truths in chess is that attacks along one wing are destined to fail if the centre is not sufficiently controlled. This is because the defender with a strong centre will generally be able to muster enough defence on that side and at the same time mount a counterattack in the centre and/or on the other wing. So if you plan on mounting an attack make sure you control the centre.

Traditionally it was thought that the ideal situation is one where you have a pawn majority in the centre, especially with pawns on d4 and e4 (for white). However it has been shown that an equally valid strategy is to control the centre with pieces and make minimal pawn moves. The thinking is that central pawn moves often lead to permanent positions and can block attacks. "Fianchettoing" a bishop by moving it to b2 or g2 after b3 or g3 allows the bishop to keep a watchful eye on the centre without fixing a pawn in the centre.

Protect the King It is not always necessary although highly advisable to protect the king through castling. That being said, there are other ways to go about protecting the king than castling although they are less efficient and will often result in pins.

section: A Few Common Openings (illustrative, not exhaustive)
text: **Italian Game**: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. A classical opening that develops a piece towards the centre and eyes the f7 square early. two common replies are 3...Bc5 (the "Giuoco Piano", Italian for "Quiet Game") and 3...Nf6.

section: A Few Common Openings (illustrative, not exhaustive)
text: **Ruy Lopez (Spanish Opening)**: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. one of the oldest and most respected openings, developing the bishop to pressure the knight defending e5.

section: A Few Common Openings (illustrative, not exhaustive)
text: **Sicilian Defence**: 1.e4 c5. The most common and highest-scoring reply to 1.e4 at all levels. Instead of mirroring White's central pawn, Black creates an asymmetrical position and often gets active piece play in return.

section: A Few Common Openings (illustrative, not exhaustive)
text: **Queen's Gambit**: 1.d4 d5 2.c4. White offers a wing pawn to gain faster development and central influence. Despite the name, white does not usually end up a pawn down for long if Black accepts it (2...dxc4).

Chess is a two-player strategy board game played on a square board with 64 squares. One player controls the white pieces and the other controls the black pieces, and the players take turns making one move at a time. There is no luck and no hidden information in chess: both players can see the whole board, so the result depends on planning and skill.
The goal of chess is to checkmate the opponent's king, which means attacking it in a way that it cannot escape. A game of chess can also end in a draw, where neither player wins.
Chess is played all over the world at home, in clubs, online and in tournaments. The official rules of chess are maintained by FIDE, the international chess federation.

section: How to play chess: the quick version
text: To play chess, set up the board with each player's 16 pieces and let White move first. The players take turns moving one piece at a time, and each type of piece moves in its own way. You capture an enemy piece by moving onto its square. If your opponent's king is attacked, that is check, and if it cannot escape it is checkmate and you win.

section: How to play chess: the quick version
text: A good way to start is to learn how each piece moves, then learn check and checkmate, then the special moves of castling, en passant and promotion, and finally the opening principles.

section: The board and the starting position
text: The chessboard has eight rows, called ranks, and eight columns, called files. Together they make 64 squares that alternate between light and dark. The board is placed so that each player has a light square in the right-hand corner closest to them.

section: The board and the starting position
text: Each player starts with 16 pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns. The pawns stand on the second row from each player and the other pieces stand behind them. The queen starts on a square of her own colour, so the white queen starts on a light square and the black queen on a dark square. White always makes the first move.

The king moves one square in any direction: forwards, backwards, sideways or diagonally. The king can never move to a square where it would be attacked. It is the most important piece because if it is checkmated the game is lost.
The queen is the most powerful piece. She moves any number of squares in a straight line along a rank, a file or a diagonal, as long as no piece is in the way.
A rook moves any number of squares in a straight line along a rank or a file, but not diagonally.
A bishop moves any number of squares diagonally. Because of this, each bishop always stays on squares of the colour it started on.
A knight moves in an L-shape: two squares in one direction and then one square to the side. The knight is the only piece that can jump over other pieces.

A pawn moves forward one square, or two squares from its starting square, and it captures one square diagonally forward. Pawns cannot move backwards. A pawn that reaches the far end of the board is promoted, usually to a queen.

Beginners use point values as a rough guide to the strength of each piece: a pawn is worth 1 point, a knight 3, a bishop 3, a rook 5 and a queen 9. The king has no point value because losing it ends the game. These numbers are only a guideline, because a strong position can matter more than counting material.

When a king is under attack it is in check. A player in check must get out of check immediately by moving the king, blocking the attack or capturing the attacking piece. It is illegal to leave your own king in check.
If a player is in check and has no way to escape, it is checkmate and the game is over. The player who delivered checkmate wins the game of chess.

A game is a draw if the player to move is not in check but has no legal move; this is called stalemate. A game is also drawn if both players agree to a draw or if neither player can possibly checkmate the other, for example with only the two kings left. A player can also resign, which means giving up and losing the game.

Castling is a special move that helps keep the king safe. The king moves two squares towards a rook and that rook jumps to the other side of the king. You can only castle if the king and that rook have not moved before, there are no pieces between them, the king is not in check, and the king does not pass through or land on a square that is attacked.

En passant is a special pawn capture. If a pawn moves two squares forward from its starting square and lands next to an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may capture it as if it had moved only one square. This must be done immediately on the very next move or the chance is lost.

section: The three phases of a chess game
text: A game of chess usually has three phases. The opening is the first moves, when players bring their pieces into play and fight for the centre. The middlegame is when most of the tactics and attacks happen. The endgame is when few pieces are left and the kings become active and pawns try to promote.

Chess moves are written in algebraic notation. The files are labelled a to h from left to right and the ranks are numbered 1 to 8 from White's side, so every square has a name such as e4. A move is written with a letter for the piece: K for king, Q for queen, R for rook, B for bishop and N for knight. Pawn moves have no letter. An x means a capture, a plus sign means check, a hash sign means checkmate, and O-O and O-O-O mean castling on the kingside and the queenside.
tactic: a short, forcing sequence of moves that wins material or gives checkmate, such as a fork, pin or skewer. A tactic is a short-term idea, while a strategy is a long-term plan.
strategy: the long-term plan for a game, such as controlling the centre, improving piece positions or creating a weakness in the opponent's position.
fork: a single piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time, so the opponent can usually save only one of them. Knights are famous for forks, but queens and pawns can fork too.

pin: a piece is pinned when it cannot or should not move because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line. In an absolute pin the piece shields the king, so moving it would be illegal. In a relative pin moving it is legal but would lose the more valuable piece.
skewer: an attack on a valuable piece that must move away, which exposes a less valuable piece behind it to capture. A skewer is like a pin in reverse.
discovered attack: moving one piece out of the way so that another piece behind it attacks something. If the revealed attack is on the enemy king, it is called a discovered check.
double check: two pieces give check at the same time. The only way to answer a double check is to move the king.

zugzwang: a position in which the player to move would like to pass but cannot, because every legal move makes their position worse. The word is German for compulsion to move, and it is most common in endgames.
gambit: an opening in which a player sacrifices a pawn, or sometimes more, to gain faster development or an attack.
sacrifice: to give up material on purpose in return for an attack, a better position or checkmate.
tempo: a unit of time in chess equal to one move. Gaining a tempo means making progress while forcing the opponent to waste a move, and losing a tempo means wasting a move.
development: moving your pieces from their starting squares to active squares where they can control the board.
fianchetto: developing a bishop to b2, g2, b7 or g7, usually after moving the knight pawn one square, so the bishop controls the long diagonal.
opposition: a king-and-pawn endgame idea in which the two kings face each other with one empty square between them. The player who has to move must step aside, which can let the other king advance.

passed pawn: a pawn with no enemy pawns in front of it on its own file or the files next to it, so no enemy pawn can block or capture it as it advances. Passed pawns are very dangerous in the endgame.
doubled pawns: two pawns of the same colour on the same file, which is usually a weakness.
isolated pawn: a pawn with no friendly pawns on the files next to it, so other pawns cannot defend it.
open file: a file with no pawns on it. Rooks are strong on open files.
back rank mate: a checkmate on a king that is trapped on its first rank by its own pawns, usually delivered by a rook or queen.
scholar's mate: a very quick checkmate in as few as four moves in which the queen and bishop attack the weak f7 square, or f2 for Black. Beginners can avoid it by defending that square.
fool's mate: the quickest possible checkmate, in only two moves, which happens only if White plays very weak moves.
exchange: trading one piece for another. Winning the exchange means winning a rook, worth 5 points, for a knight or bishop, worth 3 points.
blunder: a serious mistake that loses material or the game.
hanging piece: a piece that is attacked and not defended, so it can be captured for free.
material: the pieces and pawns each side has. Being ahead in material means having more total point value.
initiative: the ability to keep making threats so that the opponent must keep responding.
major pieces: the queens and rooks. The bishops and knights are called minor pieces.
bishop pair: having both bishops while the opponent does not. Two bishops working together are often an advantage in open positions.
kingside castling: castling with the rook on the h-file, also called short castling and written O-O.
queenside castling: castling with the rook on the a-file, also called long castling and written O-O-O.

In the opening, try to do four things. Control the centre with pawns or pieces, develop your knights and bishops quickly, castle early so your king is safe and your rook joins the game, and avoid moving the same piece twice without a good reason. Also avoid bringing your queen out too early, because enemy pieces can attack her and gain time.

Before every move, check three things. First, what is my opponent threatening with their last move? Second, are any of my pieces undefended? Third, can I check, capture or threaten something? Looking at checks, captures and threats in this order stops most beginner blunders.

In the middlegame, improve your least active piece, put rooks on open files, and keep your king safe. Look for tactics such as forks, pins and skewers, and also check whether your opponent has one. Try to avoid doubled and isolated pawns because they are hard to defend.

If you are ahead in material, trading pieces usually helps you because the extra material counts for more when the board is emptier. If you are behind, avoid trades and look for complications. Never trade without checking that the trade does not leave one of your pieces unprotected.

In the endgame the king becomes a strong piece, so bring your king towards the centre. Create a passed pawn and push it. A good rule is to place your rook behind a passed pawn. When you are ahead, be careful not to cause stalemate by leaving the enemy king with no legal move, because that is only a draw.

The most common beginner mistakes are moving too fast, leaving pieces hanging, bringing the queen out early, ignoring the opponent's threats, forgetting to castle, pushing too many pawns, and falling for scholar's mate. Slowing down and checking what the opponent just did fixes most of them.

To improve at chess, play regularly, review your games to find your mistakes, solve tactics puzzles every day, and learn the basic endgames. Learn opening principles rather than memorising long lines of moves, because the principles work in every game.
